25299833.title: 2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election
25299833.extract:
The 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election was held on November 4, 2025, to determine whether three Pennsylvania Supreme Court justices would serve additional terms. The three justices up for retention were Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht, all of whom are Democrats.

Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht are all current justices on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. They were up for a yes-or-no retention vote, where voters were asked to vote whether to give each justice another ten-year term.

Pennsylvania elects its statewide judges to 10-year terms, then holds nonpartisan "retention elections" - a simple yes or no vote - to determine whether the judges should continue serving. In the 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election, the three justices faced a simple yes-or-no question at the end of the ballot.

Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht have won additional terms on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. The election results were announced on November 4, 2025, and they were retained by a majority of voters. This outcome maintained the 5-2 Democratic majority on the state court.

Republicans, including President Donald Trump, had pushed voters to unseat the three justices as what has been a historically quiet race gained attention. Despite the push from some political figures, the justices were retained by a majority of voters.

3.title: All three PA Supreme Court justices win retention election
3.description: Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht have won additional terms on the PA Supreme Court.
3.content:
HARRISBURG —Pennsylvanians have voted to retain three Democratic state Supreme Court justices, granting them additional terms on the bench after an unusually contentious, multimillion-dollar election.

Republicans and their allies had hoped to defeat the justices and put their seats on the 2027 ballot, opening a path to flip the court. The Democratic majority has handed down critical rulings over the past decade, upholding mail voting and throwing out a congressional map that it found unfairly benefited the GOP.

Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht were on the ballot Tuesday. They were first elected in 2015 in a sweep that flipped the court from Republican to Democratic control.

The Associated Press called all three races at 9:53 p.m. Unofficial results show their margins are all around 27 points.

Superior Court Judge Alice Dubow and Commonwealth Court Judge Michael Wojcik also won their retention races on Tuesday. The Associated Press called those races shortly after 10 p.m.

Retention elections are typically low-interest, low-spending races that favor incumbents. [Only one statewide judge has lost](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/judicial-retention-supreme-court-2025-guide-elections/) their retention election since 1968, when the state constitution was last updated.

These elections provide justices with another 10 years on the bench. However, Donohue will hit the state’s mandatory retirement age of 75 in two years. That means there will be an open, partisan election to fill the vacancy in 2027. (Chief Justice Debra Todd, a Democrat, and Justice Sallie Mundy, a Republican, will be up for retention that year.)

The last state Supreme Court retention elections were held in 2017, with Todd and Thomas Saylor, a Republican who has since retired, on the ballot. Spending on those races — from [the](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20170045)[candidates](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20170017) as well as from special interests via independent expenditures — was relatively low, totaling about $850,000.

Spending this year has well exceeded that total.

Campaign finance records show nearly $3.3 million has been spent by [Dougherty](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20240446) or on his behalf through in-kind donations of goods or services like mailers through Oct. 20. That total is more than $2 million for [Wecht](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20140414) and $1.8 million for [Donohue](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20250024).

In addition, [a wide range of special interest groups](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-race-spending-independent-expenditures-elections/) — including [Planned Parenthood’s super PAC](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/retention-election-abortion-advertising-supreme-court-pennsylvania-elections/), [Democratic](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/supreme-court-pennsylvania-campaign-finance-november-election-aclu-democratic-yass-elections/) and [Republican](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election/) committees that receive national money, and a [trio of groups](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-race-spending-independent-expenditures-elections/) tied to the state’s richest man, Jeffrey Yass — have spent at least $9.8 million as of Tuesday evening.

Anti-retention groups urged voters to “term limit the court” and “defend our democracy,” and highlighted high-profile decisions, including a ruling to overturn the conviction of comedian Bill Cosby [on a technicality](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/bill-cosby-be-released-after-sexual-assault-conviction-overturned-pennsylvania-n1272748). A Yass-connected group sent out a [mailer](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-misleading-redistricting-claims-elections/) that accused the court of gerrymandering the state’s congressional map “to help Democrats win,” while highlighting a GOP-drawn map thrown out for unfairly benefiting Republicans.

Groups supporting the justices said that the state Supreme Court would defend [reproductive health care](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/retention-election-abortion-advertising-supreme-court-pennsylvania-elections/) in the state, and [argued in ads](https://adstransparency.google.com/advertiser/AR14015309208400953345/creative/CR10108323711456116737?region=US&topic=political&start-date=2025-01-01&end-date=2025-10-17) that “billionaires” are “trying to buy our independent and fair courts.”

All three justices were [recommended by the Pennsylvania Bar Association](https://www.pabar.org/site/For-Lawyers/Committees-Commissions/Judicial-Evaluation/Resources/JEC-Ratings/2025/Supreme-Court), which called them “fair,” “open to consideration of differing perspectives,” and “logical.”

Donohue worked as a civil trial lawyer and commercial litigator before being elected to the Superior Court of Pennsylvania in 2007. The Superior is one of two intermediate appellate courts in the state and largely focuses on criminal, family, and civil cases that are appealed up from the county Courts of Common Pleas.

Since her election to the state Supreme Court in 2015, Donohue has been the primary author on a number of high-profile decisions, including one in [2022](https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/2022/14-15-17-18-amp-19-map-2022.html) that upheld Pennsylvania’s no-excuse mail voting law, Act 77.

Dougherty began his career as an assistant district attorney in Philadelphia, then worked in private practice before he was appointed to the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas in 2001. He stayed in that position until his election to the state Supreme Court.

During this retention race, [he has highlighted](https://retaindougherty.com/) his work on a “statewide behavioral health initiative” that involved the establishment, last year, of an Office of Behavioral Health within the courts, and another program that created sensory-friendly courtrooms to accommodate people on the autism spectrum.

Dougherty also has notable family ties. His brother, John Dougherty, was the head of Local 98 of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers for decades before he was sentenced to six years in prison for bribing a city council member and embezzlement. His son, Sean Dougherty, is a member of the state House, serving northeast Philadelphia.

Wecht served as register of wills and clerk of the Orphans Court of Allegheny County before being elected to the county’s Court of Common Pleas. He was then elected to the Superior Court in 2011 before his election to the Supreme Court.

Among the opinions Wecht has written as a Supreme Court justice were [a contentious 2020 ruling](https://www.ballardspahr.com/-/jssmedia/files/alerts/wecht---majority.pdf?rev=a4a7bb8419dc42e990ee0a1ff514f312&hash=5901F14E2B68ED01675A029F4ACDEA40) upholding Gov. Tom Wolf’s pandemic powers, in which he argued that the “Pennsylvania Constitution does not empower the legislature to act unilaterally to suspend” [the state’s disaster law](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2020/07/pennsylvania-coronavirus-disaster-declaration-supreme-court-ruling/), from which Wolf had claimed his authority.

Pennsylvania Supreme Court Retention Race 2025
==============================================

 On November 4, three state Supreme Court justices are up for retention. These retention elections appear as a YES or NO question at the end of your ballot. 

 Share this page 

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.aclupa.org%2Fscopa2025%2F)[Post](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.aclupa.org%2Fscopa2025%2F&text=Pennsylvania%20Supreme%20Court%20Retention%20Race%202025)[Copy](https://www.aclupa.org/scopa2025/)

[](https://www.aclupa.org/scopa2025/)

![Image 5: A blue graphic with a photo of the liberty bell with text that says, "Our state supreme court is the last line of defense for our rights. November 4".](https://www.aclupa.org/app/uploads/2025/09/SCOPA-Graphic.png)

WHAT IS A RETENTION ELECTION?
-----------------------------

A **retention** election is a **nonpartisan** process for voters to decide whether to **retain** (or keep) an elected official in office by casting a **YES** or **NO** vote.

In Pennsylvania, state Supreme Court justices serve 10-year terms. They are first elected in a **partisan** election, and at the end of each term, they face a **retention** election.

WHAT DOES A YES OR NO VOTE MEAN IN A RETENTION ELECTION?
--------------------------------------------------------

A **YES** vote keeps the current state Supreme Court in place.

A **NO** vote triggers a two-year partisan process to elect a new justice.

WHY ARE THESE ELECTIONS IMPORTANT?
----------------------------------

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court decides many important cases that affect our daily lives. Make sure you make a plan to vote!

![Image 6: Signs that spell out vote on the grass in front of a large brown brick building that is surrounded by red and blue balloons.](https://www.aclupa.org/app/uploads/2025/09/Election-Day-2024-for-ACLU-Afternoon-11-1-scaled.jpg)

*   **Wednesday, November 12, 2025:**Last day for county boards of elections to receive completed military and overseas absentee ballots (submitted for delivery no later than 11:59 p.m. on November 3, 2025)

[Find your polling place here](https://www.pavoterservices.pa.gov/Pages/PollingPlaceInfo.aspx)

Live Results: Pennsylvania Supreme Court 2025 election
======================================================

[Politics](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics) Updated on Nov 19, 2025 11:43 AM EST — Published on Nov 3, 2025 12:02 PM EST 

* * *

WASHINGTON (AP) — Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Kevin Dougherty was retained by Pennsylvania voters on Tuesday.

[**READ MORE:** Pennsylvania reelects Supreme Court justices, maintaining Democratic majority](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/pennsylvania-reelects-supreme-court-justices-maintaining-democratic-majority)

It was a victory for Democrats, who were backing Dougherty and two other justices in a campaign to maintain a 5-2 Democratic majority on the court.

Pennsylvania elects its statewide judges to 10-year terms, then holds nonpartisan “retention elections” — a simple yes or no vote — to determine whether the judge will serve another term. Dougherty has served on the state Supreme Court since 2016.

The Associated Press declared Dougherty was retained at 9:51 p.m. EST.

* * *

WASHINGTON (AP) — Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice David Wecht was retained by Pennsylvania voters on Tuesday.

The vote is a victory for Democrats, who campaigned to keep Wecht and two other justices on the court to maintain its 5-2 Democratic majority.

[**WATCH:** Why Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court election has national implications](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/why-pennsylvanias-supreme-court-election-has-national-implications)

Pennsylvania elects its statewide judges to 10-year terms, then holds nonpartisan “retention elections” — a simple yes or no vote — to determine whether the judge will serve another term.

Wecht has served on the state Supreme Court since 2016.

The Associated Press declared Wecht retained at 9:51 EST.

* * *

WASHINGTON (AP) — Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Christine Donohue was retained by Pennsylvania voters on Tuesday.

The state’s Supreme Court had a 5-2 Democratic majority entering Tuesday’s election. Republicans campaigned to try to stop three judges up for retention — Donohue and two others — from continuing on the court. The state Democratic Party backed Donohue in her bid for retention.

Pennsylvania elects its statewide judges to 10-year terms, then holds nonpartisan “retention elections” — a simple yes or no vote — to determine whether the judge will serve another term. Donohue has served on the state Supreme Court since 2016. With the vote, Donohue may remain on the court until she reaches mandatory retirement age in 2027.

The Associated Press declared Donohue was retained at 9:51 p.m. EST.

6.title: A Nonpartisan Guide to the 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court Retention Election - Guides.vote | Voters Guides
6.description: To download a PDF of this guide in English, click here,
6.content:
_To download a PDF of this guide in English, click[here](https://guides.vote/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Pennsylvania-Supreme-Court-2025-6-6-25.pdf),_

Three seats on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court are up for a retention election on November 4. A retention election is simple: Voters are asked to vote Yes or No as to whether to give each justice another ten-year term. The Court has seven justices; currently five are Democrats, and two are Republicans. The three justices up for re-election are all Democrats. If at least two of the justices fail to win retention, that could shift majority control. Both parties have been [preparing](https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2024-12-23/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-political-fight) for a hard-fought election.

The Court decides questions of state law that can have significant impact. In recent years, among other decisions the Court ruled [that](https://www.pghcitypaper.com/news/pa-supreme-court-says-warrantless-searches-not-justified-by-cannabis-smell-alone-20837777) warrantless searches are not justified if they are based solely on the smell of cannabis; [that](https://statecourtreport.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/pa_sc_genser.pdf) citizens have a right to vote by provisional ballot if their mail-in ballot is disqualified for a failure to return it in the required secrecy envelope; and [that](https://www.eff.org/files/2019/11/20/commonwealth_v._davis_-_majority_opinion.pdf) the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution protects people from being forced to hand over their digital passwords.

To help you understand this election, we’ve assembled background on the justices’ written opinions and votes in key cases before the Court, along with their public statements, education, and previous work experience, to indicate how they might rule on key issues in the future.

**CHRISTINE DONOHUE**
---------------------

*   **On abortion,** Donohue [wrote](https://apnews.com/article/pennsylvania-abortion-391844f5b4d9b197400abe8803280133), “the Pennsylvania Constitution secures the fundamental right to reproductive autonomy.” And that “includes a right to decide whether to have an abortion or to carry a pregnancy to term.”
*   **On education,** she [agreed](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/J-82-2016mo.pdf?cb=2) that a lower court should hold a trial on whether state officials are failing to adequately and equitably fund public education.
*   **On gun policy**, in a dispute over a city’s restriction on the location of gun ranges, Donohue [wrote](https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/2024/68-map-2022-0.html) that “engaging in firearms proficiency training on… private residential property is not covered” in “the Second Amendment.”
*   **On LGBTQ rights,** Donohue [wrote](https://epgn.com/2015/05/07/sounding-off-where-pa-supreme-court-candidates-stand-on-lgbt-issues/), “As judges we must educate ourselves on all LGBT issues, including the insidious nature of crimes directed at members of the LGBT community.”
*   **On marijuana,** Donohue [agreed](https://www.mcall.com/2021/12/29/marijuana-odor-alone-not-enough-reason-to-search-vehicle-pa-supreme-court-rules-in-allentown-case/) that given medical marijuana’s legal status in Pennsylvania, the smell of marijuana cannot be the sole reason for a warrantless vehicle search. She also [agreed](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/J-42-2020mo%20-%20104458522103461826.pdf?cb=1) that people under court supervision should be allowed to use medical marijuana.
*   **On redistricting,** she [agreed](https://pubintlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/2018-02-07-Majority-Opinion.pdf) that the state legislature’s 2011 redistricting plan was an unconstitutional gerrymander.
*   **On voting,** Donohue [ruled](https://statecourtreport.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/pa_sc_genser.pdf) that when a voter’s mail-in ballot is rejected because of a disqualifying mistake, that voter must still be allowed to cast a provisional ballot on election day.
*   **On voting,** she [opposed](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/136MM2024ds%20-%20106152930288599429.pdf) a [ruling](https://www.npr.org/2024/11/18/nx-s1-5195524/pennsylvania-election-ballots-senate-recount) throwing out mail-in ballots that didn’t have the correct date.

**Christine Donohue**[was elected](https://donohue2025.com/meet-christine/) to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court in 2015. She earned her bachelor’s degree from East Stroudsburg University, and her law degree from Duquesne University School of Law. She was in private law practice for 27 years at a civil trial lawyer and litigator. She was [elected](https://www.pacourts.us/courts/supreme-court/supreme-court-justices/justice-christine-donohue) judge of the Pennsylvania Superior Court in 2007.

**Area of personal interest:** With increasing difficulty for young trial attorneys to get training in basic advocacy skills, she [initiated](https://projectlitigate.org/about) an “[effort](https://donohue2025.com/meet-christine/) by trial judges and lawyers to afford young lawyers opportunities to gain courtroom experience, especially presenting cases to civil juries.”

* * *

**KEVIN DOUGHERTY**
-------------------

*   **On abortion,** Dougherty [agreed](https://apnews.com/article/pennsylvania-abortion-391844f5b4d9b197400abe8803280133) that a lower court must hear a challenge to a law that limited the use of Medicaid funding to cover abortions. He has not indicated whether the Pennsylvania Constitution guarantees a fundamental right to abortion.
*   **On education,** he [wrote](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/j-82-2016co.pdf) that the Court had a clear duty to consider whether Pennsylvania citizens’ Constitutional rights to “a proper public education” are being violated by [inadequate funding](https://thephiladelphiacitizen.org/guest-commentary-the-pending-supreme-court-bombshell/).
*   **On gun policy,** Dougherty [wrote](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/J-29-2023mo%20-%20105840172255863439.pdf) that a city’s restriction on the location of gun ranges is “consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation” and “outside the Second Amendment’s unqualified command.”
*   **On LGBTQ rights,** about the decision allowing same-sex couples to adopt children in PA, Dougherty [said](https://lancasteronline.com/news/local/get-to-know-the-candidates-for-state-supreme-court/article_65c426d4-6d45-11e5-b74f-6babb36c03bb.html), “We have hundreds of thousands of children sitting in out-of-home placement, wishing they had a permanent and loving family. That one decision permitted many, many, many, many, many children to find loving homes. That’s phenomenal, the impact of one decision.”
*   **On marijuana,** he [agreed](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/J-42-2020mo%20-%20104458522103461826.pdf?cb=1) that people under court supervision should be allowed to use medical marijuana.
*   **On mental health issues** in the justice system, he [said,](https://www.wgal.com/article/wgal-8-in-focus-justice-kevin-dougherty/44107140) “We don’t have to lock people up because they have mental illness or because they are different. We need to be able to find out what the root cause is and divert them, particularly veterans. I’m a strong supporter of veteran courts.”
*   **On redistricting,** Dougherty [agreed](https://pubintlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/2018-02-07-Majority-Opinion.pdf) that the state legislature’s 2011 redistricting plan was an unconstitutional gerrymander.
*   **On voting,**he [agreed](https://wwwsecure.pacourts.us/Storage/media/pdfs/20241023/213545-oct.23,2024-concurringopinion.pdf) that when a voter’s mail-in ballot is rejected, that voter’s provisional ballot must still [be counted](https://statecourtreport.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/pa_sc_genser.pdf).

**Kevin Dougherty**[was elected](https://retaindougherty.com/meet-kevin/) to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court in 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree from Temple University, and his law degree from Antioch School of Law. An assistant [district attorney](https://www.pacourts.us/courts/supreme-court/supreme-court-justices/justice-kevin-m-dougherty) in Phila. County from 1990 to 1995 and then in private law practice, he served from 2001 to 2015 in the Phila. County Court of Common Pleas.

**Area of personal interest:** he supports [having](https://www.fox43.com/article/news/local/pennsylvania-supreme-court-autism-in-the-courts-progress-report/521-116b77f1-b373-4150-ba50-504e32c79985) “a conversation about autism in our courts.” “If your [behaviors](https://www.abc27.com/news/top-stories/state-supreme-court-justice-focuses-on-autism-in-courtrooms/) are something you can’t control because of a neurological complexity, then maybe I [as a [judge](https://apnews.com/general-news-b199913b756a1d96c15f6c5373c530c3)] should be a little more sensitive to that if I want to do the right thing.”

* * *

**DAVID WECHT**
---------------

*   **On abortion,** Wecht [wrote](https://davidwecht.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Allegheny-Reproductive-Health-Concurring-Opinion-Wecht.pdf) that women have a “right to reproductive autonomy.” “The Pennsylvania Constitution’s ERA did away with the antiquated and misogynistic notion that a woman has no say over what happens to her own body.”
*   **On education,** he [ordered](https://www.elc-pa.org/cases/william-penn-sd-et-al-v-pa-dept-of-education-et-al-pa-2017/) a lower court to hold a trial on whether state officials are failing to adequately and equitably fund public education. He [saw validity](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/J-82-2016mo.pdf?cb=2) in the claim that “distribution of state funds results in widespread deprivations in economically disadvantaged districts,” limiting “the resources necessary to attain a constitutionally adequate education.”
*   **On gun policy,** Wecht [agreed](https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/2024/68-map-2022.html) that a city’s restriction on the location of gun ranges is “consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”
*   **On LGBTQ rights,** he [is a](https://epgn.com/2015/10/29/out-at-the-polls-judicial-and-row-offices/) “firm believer in equality” and was “personally thrilled” when same-sex marriage was legalized.
*   **On marijuana,** Wecht [agreed](https://www.mcall.com/2021/12/29/marijuana-odor-alone-not-enough-reason-to-search-vehicle-pa-supreme-court-rules-in-allentown-case/) that given medical marijuana’s legal status in Pennsylvania, the smell of marijuana cannot be the sole reason for a warrantless vehicle search. He also [agreed](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/Supreme/out/J-42-2020mo%20-%20104458522103461826.pdf?cb=1) that people under court supervision should be allowed to use medical marijuana.
*   **On redistricting,** he [agreed](https://pubintlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/2018-02-07-Majority-Opinion.pdf) that the state legislature’s 2011 redistricting plan was an unconstitutional gerrymander.
*   **On voting,** Wecht [opposed](https://wwwsecure.pacourts.us/Storage/media/pdfs/20241023/213724-oct.23,2024-dissentingopinion2.pdf) a decision allowing a voter’s election-day provisional ballot to be counted when that voter’s mail-in ballot had a disqualifying mistake, such as failure to place a returned ballot in a [secrecy envelope](https://statecourtreport.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/pa_sc_genser.pdf).

**David Wecht**[was elected](https://davidwecht.com/meet-david/) to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court in 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree in history and political science from Yale University and his law degree from Yale Law School. He [was](https://www.pacourts.us/courts/supreme-court/supreme-court-justices/justice-david-n-wecht) in private law practice from 1989 to 2003, and then was a judge in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas until 2012. He was elected judge of the Pennsylvania Superior Court in 2012.

**Area of personal interest:** In light of his concern about anti-Semitism, he [says](https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/arts-letters/articles/justice-david-wecht-antisemitism) we should not “eliminate or place incursions on the First Amendment…. It’s critical that we never in this country give government the power to pick and choose which speech is preferred. The remedy for hate speech is more speech.”

* * *

[**guides.vote**](https://guides.vote/)is a nonpartisan effort to show where candidates stand. We do not support or oppose any political party or candidate. See [**Vote411.org**](https://vote411.org/)for information on how to vote. For campuses, see Campus Vote Project’s [**state-specific guides**](https://campusvoteproject.org/state-student-voting-guides/) to student voting rules.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election![Image 2: A 60x44 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Flag_of_Pennsylvania.svg/60px-Flag_of_Pennsylvania.svg.png)

* * *

The **2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election** was held on November 4, 2025, to determine whether 3 [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Pennsylvania "Supreme Court of Pennsylvania") justices would serve their second 10-year terms. [Christine Donohue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Donohue "Christine Donohue"), [Kevin Dougherty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Dougherty "Kevin Dougherty"), and [David Wecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wecht "David Wecht"), who were first elected as [Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election "2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election"), were all retained by large margins, including in over a dozen counties[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-1) won by [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2)

The [Supreme Court of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Pennsylvania "Supreme Court of Pennsylvania") currently has a 5-2 Democratic majority.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-3) The court has been [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")-controlled since [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election "2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election"), when [Donohue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Donohue "Christine Donohue"), [Dougherty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Dougherty "Kevin Dougherty"), and [Wecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wecht "David Wecht") won election to their seats.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-4)

Had voters chosen not to retain any of the justices, [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania")[Josh Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Shapiro "Josh Shapiro") could have appointed a temporary replacement until 2027 — with approval from two-thirds of the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")-controlled [Pennsylvania Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Senate "Pennsylvania State Senate")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Guardian1-5) — when an election would have been held for a permanent replacement.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-6) If all three justices were not retained and the Senate did not approve Shapiro's nominees, the court would be split with two Democrats and two Republicans, which _[The Philadelphia Inquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Philadelphia\_Inquirer "The Philadelphia Inquirer")_ claimed could leave the court "unlikely to reach majority decisions and could weaken the voice of Pennsylvania's top court going into the [2028 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election "2028 United States presidential election"), when the [swing state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state") could decide the next president yet again."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-7)

Since [retention elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retention_election "Retention election") were established in 1968, only one Pennsylvania justice, [Russell Nigro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_M._Nigro "Russell M. Nigro") in [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Pennsylvania_elections "2005 Pennsylvania elections"), has not been retained.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-8)

The justices themselves were not permitted to directly campaign. Instead, they engaged in a statewide speaking tour where they pledged to exercise their judicial power without [partisan bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partisan_bias "Partisan bias").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-9)_[The Philadelphia Inquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Philadelphia\_Inquirer "The Philadelphia Inquirer")_ said that over $14 million had been raised in support of retention,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-10) while the [Brennan Center for Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_Center_for_Justice "Brennan Center for Justice") estimated that $7.5 million has been spent by liberal political action committees on TV ads in support of a 'Yes' vote to "protect elections and preserve abortion rights". They also claimed that the race was the second most expensive retention election in U.S. history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Gaz-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-12)

Deborah Gross, executive director of the non-profit Pennsylvanians for Modern Courts, claimed that the significant spending 'perverts the intent of the retention process' by focusing on party affiliation rather than the justices' records. Talking to the _[Pennsylvania Capital-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania\_Capital-Star "Pennsylvania Capital-Star")_, Gross said, "[i]f someone is not doing their job properly, if they're not showing up for court, if they're doing bad acts, if they have judicial conduct issues. Those are reasons why someone should not be retained."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-13)

The [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") announced a "six-figure investment" into the [Pennsylvania Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Democratic_Party "Pennsylvania Democratic Party") to help support retaining the 3 judges,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Dems-14) with [DNC Chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_chairs_of_the_Democratic_National_Committee "List of chairs of the Democratic National Committee")[Ken Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Martin "Ken Martin") issuing a statement saying that "[t]he Pennsylvania Supreme Court is on the frontlines of decisions related to voting rights, redistricting, abortion protections" and that "[t]he stakes couldn't be higher."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Dems-14)

The state and national chapters of the [ACLU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_Liberties_Union "American Civil Liberties Union") spent $500,000 on a mail campaign to inform voters about the race "and what it means for their civil rights and civil liberties." The organization's website did not make an explicit case for or against retaining any of the judges.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-15)

Conservative activist [Scott Presler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Presler "Scott Presler") told _[Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox\_News "Fox News")_ that his [PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee"), Early Vote Action, was targeting [Bucks County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucks_County,_Pennsylvania "Bucks County, Pennsylvania") — which voted [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania") for the first time in almost [four decades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_United_States_presidential_election "1988 United States presidential election") — by sending 100,000 text messages as part of a campaign that recognizes [Charlie Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Kirk "Charlie Kirk")’s birthday. Presler also stated that the group was producing stickers that say 'I voted in honor of Charlie' with a "really classy photo" of Kirk with his hands together in prayer.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Fox-16) Bucks County chose to retain all 3 justices by over 20 points.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2)

Multiple PACs affiliated with Republican businessman [Matthew Brouillette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Brouillette "Matthew Brouillette") and funded almost entirely by billionaire [Jeff Yass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Yass "Jeff Yass") — a registered [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_of_Pennsylvania "Libertarian Party of Pennsylvania") — spent millions on social media ads, mailers, and text messages opposing retaining all 3 judges, telling voters they should “term limit the woke Democrat Pennsylvania Supreme Court.”[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-W-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-NOTUS1-18)

The Commonwealth Leaders Fund, a Yass-affiliated PAC, was criticized by the advocacy group Fair Districts PA after they sent out mailers claiming that the "liberal Supreme Court gerrymandered our congressional districts to help Democrats win." The mailers also featured an outdated image of 2 [congressional districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_House_of_Representatives "Pennsylvania House of Representatives") from a map that was drawn up by the Republican-controlled [state legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_General_Assembly "Pennsylvania General Assembly") in 2011 and later overturned for partisan [gerrymandering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrymandering "Gerrymandering") that disproportionately benefitted the Republican Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-W-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-19)

After the mailer controversy was publicized, [Pennsylvania Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Democratic_Party "Pennsylvania Democratic Party") chair [Eugene DePasquale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_DePasquale "Eugene DePasquale") issued a statement condemning "MAGA billionaires" for funneling money into the election.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-PAD-20) In late September, 2025, the [Pennsylvania Working Families Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Families_Party "Working Families Party") organized a protest outside [Susquehanna International Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susquehanna_International_Group "Susquehanna International Group"), a financial trading company founded by [Jeff Yass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Yass "Jeff Yass"), criticizing his involvement in the campaign and urging passers-by to "Vote 'Yes', not Yass".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-PAD-20)

The [League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Women_Voters "League of Women Voters") declined to endorse for or against retention, though they criticized the leading 'No' campaign PACs for misleading voters by including inaccurate information on their campaign mailers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-21) In 2017, the group argued in a [lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Women_Voters_of_Pennsylvania_v._Commonwealth_of_Pennsylvania "League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania v. Commonwealth of Pennsylvania") that Republican-gerrymandered maps violate the [state constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Constitution "Pennsylvania Constitution")'s guarantee of free and fair elections. The state Supreme Court, which included the 3 justices up for retention, ruled in favor of the claim.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Gaz-11)

The voter registration deadline was set for October 20, 2025, two weeks before the election.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-AFJ-22) With limited exceptions, ballots had to be received by 8pm on election day to be counted.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-DP2-23)[Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") permits the use of [mail-in ballots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting_in_the_United_States "Postal voting in the United States"),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-AFJ-22) including [no-excuse postal votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting_in_the_United_States#No-excuse_postal_voting "Postal voting in the United States"), allowing any registered voter to request a mail-in ballot.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-24)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-AFJ-22) However, state law prohibits [pre-processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting_in_the_United_States#Pre-processing_of_mail-in_ballots "Postal voting in the United States") of received mail-in ballots, meaning election officials had to wait until election day to begin [ballot curing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballot_curing "Ballot curing").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-25)

Republican activists and politicians urged voters to cast mail-in ballots before election day, despite [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump")'s repeated support for a ban on mail-in voting.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ABC2-26) The [Pennsylvania Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Republican_Party "Pennsylvania Republican Party") encouraged voters to request an [absentee ballot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absentee_ballot "Absentee ballot"), posting on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") that "if there is even a 1% chance that you might miss the 2025 Election, sign up for a mail-in ballot today! It's quick and easy!"[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ABC2-26)

Increased Republican support for mail-in voting was also seen in the [New Jersey gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_Jersey_gubernatorial_election "2025 New Jersey gubernatorial election"), where unsuccessful Republican candidate [Jack Ciattarelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ciattarelli "Jack Ciattarelli") boasted that "more Republicans [have] return[ed] vote-by-mail ballots than ever before."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-27) Similarly, the [California Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Republican_Party "California Republican Party") urged the use of mail-in ballots to vote against [Proposition 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_California_Proposition_50 "2025 California Proposition 50"), a ballot measure that permitted redrawing the state's congressional districts.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ABC2-26)

Despite all three justices [originally running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election "2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election") as Democrats, retention elections are considered [nonpartisan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-partisan_democracy "Non-partisan democracy"), meaning that ballots do not feature a candidate's party affiliation.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-WJFF-28)_[Votebeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Votebeat "Votebeat")_ spoke to a voter who expressed frustration over this, saying that they weren’t immediately sure if the justices were Republicans or Democrats. [Chris Borick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Borick "Chris Borick"), a professor of political science at [Muhlenberg College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhlenberg_College "Muhlenberg College"), told _Votebeat_ that the removal of partisan designation on a retention ballot can confuse voters.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Carter1-29)

### Chester County provisional ballots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chester County provisional ballots")]

On election day, _[NBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC\_News "NBC News")_ reported that [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_voter "Independent voter") and unaffiliated voters in [Chester County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_County,_Pennsylvania "Chester County, Pennsylvania") were forced to cast [provisional ballots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_ballot "Provisional ballot") after [poll books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poll_books "Poll books") listing only Republicans and Democrats were delivered to polling sites, meaning that independent voters didn't appear as registered voters, and their ballots were only counted after election officials were able to prove their eligibility.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-NBC2-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-31) A county spokeswoman later confirmed that voters registered as [Libertarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") or [Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_the_United_States "Green Party of the United States") were also forced to cast their votes with provisional ballots.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-DailyLoc1-32)

Chester County posted on social media that "supplemental poll books" were sent out to 230 polling sites, allowing voters to vote normally throughout the afternoon and evening.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-NBC2-30) A judge later extended polling hours in the county until 10pm rather than 8pm to allow impacted voters to cast non-provisional ballots.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-33)

Two weeks after election day, _[Spotlight PA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotlight\_PA "Spotlight PA")_ confirmed that roughly 11,200 of the 12,600 provisional ballots used in Chester County were counted in the final tally.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ChesterSpotlight-34) The newspaper also reported that the Republican Committee of Chester County challenged around 1,400 provisional ballots, some of which were missing signatures from voters or poll workers.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-DailyLoc1-32)

In a hearing on November 17, 2025, the Republican Committee dropped most of their objections, with the exception of ballots received in unsigned envelopes, and ballots that had no envelopes at all.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ChesterSpotlight-34) The Chester County [Board of Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Elections "Board of Elections"), who held the hearing, voted 2-1 to accept ballots where the voter had not signed the envelope in the correct place, as well as signed ballots that were received without envelopes. The board also voted unanimously to reject three unsigned ballots without envelopes.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-DailyLoc1-32) Some 300 other provisional ballots were rejected for other reasons, including a number of ballots filled out by unregistered voters.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ChesterSpotlight-34)

That same day, Chester County officials announced they had hired a law firm to investigate the missing poll books.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-WHYYChester-35) According to _[CBS News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS\_News "CBS News")_, investigators will interview county staff and examine current election processes prior to making their final recommendations for improvement at a public meeting scheduled to be held sometime in January 2026.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CBSChes-36)

[Kevin Dougherty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Dougherty "Kevin Dougherty") was first elected in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election "2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election"), and assumed office the year after. He began his law career as an assistant district attorney at the [Philadelphia District Attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Attorney_of_Philadelphia "District Attorney of Philadelphia")’s Office, before going into private practice. He was later be appointed to the [Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Court_of_Common_Pleas "Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas"), becoming administrative judge and overseeing reforms.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Running-37)

Like both other judges up for retention, Dougherty sided with the majority in the 2024 abortion ruling and the case that deemed Pennsylvania's school funding system unconstitutional.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-70)

In 2024, Dougherty authored the decision that upheld [Stroud Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroud_Township,_Pennsylvania "Stroud Township, Pennsylvania")'s restrictions on where gun ranges can be located.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Running-37) Dougherty also spearheaded the creation of the Office of Behavioral Health, who seek to improve outcomes for those in the criminal justice system with behavioral or mental health issues.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Courts-71)

> _"Mental health challenges are no longer a quiet issue on the sidelines; they are a full-blown crisis affecting every part of life in Pennsylvania."_[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Courts-71)

— Justice Kevin Dougherty

Dougherty has also led initiatives to create more inclusive courtrooms for people with sensory issues.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-72)

[David Wecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wecht "David Wecht") was first elected in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election "2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election"), and assumed office the year after. Wecht began his law career clerking for Judge [George MacKinnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_MacKinnon "George MacKinnon") on the [U.S. Court of Appeals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_Appeals "U.S. Court of Appeals") in Washington, D.C.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Running-37)

He founded a private practice in 1996, and later served on the [Superior Court of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_Court_of_Pennsylvania "Superior Court of Pennsylvania").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Running-37)

Wecht sided with the majority in the 2024 abortion ruling, writing a [concurring opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurring_opinion "Concurring opinion"), and stating that he agreed with the Majority that, "under the Equal Rights Amendment to the Pennsylvania Constitution, a sex-based distinction is presumptively unconstitutional."[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-75)

> _"The [Pennsylvania Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania\_Constitution "Pennsylvania Constitution")’s [Equal Rights Amendment][[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025\_Pennsylvania\_Supreme\_Court\_election#cite\_note-76) did away with the antiquated and misogynistic notion that a woman has no say over what happens to her own body."_[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Running-37)

— Justice David Wecht

Wecht also voted to uphold former governor [Tom Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Wolf "Tom Wolf")'s [emergency powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_powers "Emergency powers") in 2020 during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-77) In a November 2020 lawsuit challenging [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s [victory in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2020 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania"), Wecht asserted that the attempt to overturn the results of the election was "futile" and "a dangerous game."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-78)

Analysis of results
-------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Analysis of results")]

[![Image 15: Map of Pennsylvania counties shaded by winner of the 2020 U.S. presidential election](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election_results_compared_to_Trump%27s_performance_in_2024.svg/330px-Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election_results_compared_to_Trump%27s_performance_in_2024.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election_results_compared_to_Trump%27s_performance_in_2024.svg)

The justices were retained by large margins, with over 60% of the votes on all three ballot questions being in favor of retention. 16 counties[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-80) that voted for [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in the [2024 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania") chose to retain all three justices.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ResultsAnalysisInq-81)

Anti-retention campaigners heavily targeted [Bucks County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucks_County,_Pennsylvania "Bucks County, Pennsylvania"), which the Democrats had carried for 8 consecutive elections before it was won by Trump in 2024 by less than three hundred votes.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-PresR-82)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Fox-16) The county voted to retain each of the justices with margins of over 20 points.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2)

In [Northumberland County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_County,_Pennsylvania "Northumberland County, Pennsylvania"), which Trump carried by 40 points in 2024, voters chose to retain only one justice, [Kevin Dougherty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Dougherty "Kevin Dougherty").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2) In [Union County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_County,_Pennsylvania "Union County, Pennsylvania"), where a Democratic candidate has not been backed at the presidential level since [1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1832_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "1832 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania"), all three justices were retained by an average of approximately 8%.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-83)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2)

Though [Northeastern Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_Pennsylvania "Northeastern Pennsylvania") has reliably voted Republican on the presidential level for decades, the three justices outperformed [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") in counties like [Luzerne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzerne_County,_Pennsylvania "Luzerne County, Pennsylvania") and [Montour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montour_County,_Pennsylvania "Montour County, Pennsylvania"), both of which chose to retain the three justices on 10 point margins despite Trump carrying them by 20 points.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-PresR-82)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-CNNResults-2)[Chris Borick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Borick "Chris Borick"), director of the [Muhlenberg College Institute of Public Opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhlenberg_College_Institute_of_Public_Opinion "Muhlenberg College Institute of Public Opinion"), told _[The Philadelphia Inquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Philadelphia\_Inquirer "The Philadelphia Inquirer")_ that Democratic or independent voters upset with the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Trump_administration "Second Trump administration") were more motivated to vote than they previously were, while Republican voters had a lower turnout compared to 2024.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-ResultsAnalysisInq-81)

Despite the heavy spending, many voters reported that they had seen little political messaging leading up to the election.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Carter1-29) Speaking to _[Votebeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Votebeat "Votebeat")_, some voters in favor of retention said they wanted to send a message to [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") when casting their ballots, though few voters claimed to be familiar with the justices' specific rulings.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Carter1-29) A representative from One Pennsylvania, a progressive non-profit, said the vote was a rejection of [Jeff Yass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Yass "Jeff Yass") and "the MAGA agenda."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Aftermath-84)

After the election was called, Justice Donohue released a statement saying that the result shows that "Pennsylvanians have trust in the independence of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court and, additionally, appreciate the importance of a stable Pennsylvania Supreme Court."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-85) Governor [Josh Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Shapiro "Josh Shapiro") called the results "a resounding message" of support, and that "the good people of Pennsylvania will always stand for freedom."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Aftermath-84)

Former [U.S. Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General")[Eric Holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Holder "Eric Holder"), who endorsed all three justices for retention, stated that the result "demonstrates that an engaged citizenry is more powerful than the billionaires and special interests,"[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-86) while [DNC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") chair [Ken Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Martin "Ken Martin"), who actively campaigned in support of retention, said the election was a victory for [reproductive rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_rights "Reproductive rights") and voting rights, claiming that "Pennsylvania delivered a message on behalf of the entire country: No matter how rich you are, and no matter how much power you think you might have, our courts are not for sale."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_election#cite_note-Aftermath-84)

9.title: Democrats Retain Control of Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court with Three-Seat Sweep
9.content:
Three Democratic justices on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court have defeated an unusually [high-profile](https://boltsmag.org/pennsylvania-supreme-court-elections-2025/) Republican bid to unseat them. They secured large statewide victories on Tuesday, following an historically expensive campaign centered largely on the court’s role in defending voting and abortion rights.

The results preserve Democratic control of this all-important court for at least two more years. Barring any unexpected retirements, Democrats will enjoy a 5-2 majority until the next Pennsylvania Supreme Court elections, which are slated for 2027.

And Tuesday’s results mean that Republicans are now unlikely to win an outright majority until 2029 at the earliest; the best they could hope for in two years is to force a tie on the court.

Conservatives [made no secret](https://x.com/ScottPresler/status/1899900606581461212) that they were hoping to take back the court in time for the next presidential race. In this most populous of swing states, the supreme court has in recent years ruled against Republicans in several high-stakes election lawsuits. Since flipping the court in 2015, the Democratic majority has struck down a Republican gerrymander, upheld mail-in voting against conservative attacks, and rejected every one of Donald Trump’s Pennsylvania lawsuits to invalidate the 2020 presidential election.

“The projected victory for the three of us speaks well of our democracy,” one of the winning justices, David Wecht, told _Bolts_ on Tuesday night. “We all campaigned on the basis of vindicating the Pennsylvania constitution’s free and equal elections clause, and we’re all committed to continuing to vindicate that right.”

Sign up and stay up-to-date
---------------------------

The Pennsylvania justices’ victories on Tuesday, which came on a [strong](https://www.npr.org/2025/11/04/nx-s1-5589144/election-results-virginia-governor-spanberger)[night](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5587203-mikie-sherrill-democrat-victory/) for Democrats across the country, strengthens liberal dominance in the three so-called “Blue Wall” swing states: Michigan Democrats [swept](https://boltsmag.org/state-supreme-court-results-2024/) two supreme court races last fall and expanded their majority further this year thanks to a Republican justice’s retirement; and in Wisconsin, liberals [retained control](https://boltsmag.org/wisconsin-supreme-court-result-2025/) after a hard-fought campaign this spring.

Joining Wecht on the Pennsylvania ballot were justices Christine Donohue and Kevin Dougherty. Results late Tuesday showed each justice with about 60 percent support, though votes remain to be counted.

These justices were standing for retention, meaning none of them faced any opponents, and voters had to make simple yes-or-no votes on each _._ Though all three justices were initially elected as Democrats, retention races are officially nonpartisan in Pennsylvania, so there was no party ID on the ballot.

In a typical cycle, these three retention elections may not have drawn much attention; judicial retention elections here and across the country tend to overwhelmingly favor incumbents, and opponents rarely expend much time or money trying to disrupt that status quo. Only one state judge has ever lost retention in Pennsylvania, back in 2005, amid a [scandal](https://penncapital-star.com/government-politics/two-decades-after-pay-raise-scandal-rocked-harrisburg-lasting-reform-remains-elusive/) over a controversial plan lawmakers had passed to give major pay raises to government officials, including judges. Every state judge since 2005 has won by at least a 22-point margin.

But Republicans were determined this year to buck this trend, mounting a well-funded campaign to convince voters to vote against the three justices. Much of their money came from conservative billionaire [Jeff Yass](https://whyy.org/articles/pa-elections-democrats-jeffrey-yass-spending-judicial/), the richest man in Pennsylvania, plus the Republican State Leadership Committee. Conservatives flooded Pennsylvania mailboxes for weeks with a slew of mailers and ads urging “no” votes.

Democrats and their supporters responded in force, swamping airwaves and mailboxes themselves, and ultimately outspending the anti-retention campaign. Their appeal to voters included a strong focus on [abortion rights](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/retention-election-abortion-advertising-supreme-court-pennsylvania-elections/), following this court’s ruling last year that abortion restrictions amount to sex-based discrimination; the decision, authored by Donohue, was a [significant victory](https://statecourtreport.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/pennsylvania-supreme-court-ruling-overturns-decades-old-precedent) for those who support reproductive rights.

![Image 1: Man in a gray suit speaks into a microphone to a crowd of people seated in chairs in front of him in Benbow Hall](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/IMG_3145-2400x1800.jpg)

Justice Kevin Dougherty, one of three justices who secured retention on Tuesday (Alex Burness/Bolts)

As of late October, total spending in the race [had topped $14 million](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-race-pennsylvania-campaign-funding-20251102.html), easily setting the record for the most expensive judicial retention election in Pennsylvania history. The spending, sure to rise as final figures are reported after Election Day, already makes this one of the nation’s most expensive retention elections ever.

None of these justices has faced a public scandal for the GOP to build a campaign around, and certainly nothing approaching the controversy that in 2005 brought down the only Pennsylvania state judge who ever lost a retention election. So, Republicans instead tried a kitchen-sink approach, including blaming the justices for gerrymandering the state in [deceptive mailers](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-misleading-redistricting-claims-elections/) depicting an unbalanced map that, in fact, had been drawn by the GOP. Republican groups also tried to paint the justices as a threat to “women and children” because the court [overturned](https://www.npr.org/2021/06/30/1011799764/bill-cosbys-conviction-for-sexual-assault-is-overturned-by-a-pennsylvania-court) Bill Cosby’s sexual assault conviction. ([The Cosby ruling](https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2021/06/bill-cosby-bruce-castor-pennsylvania-supreme-court.html) was based on the justices’ finding of prosecutorial misconduct in his case.)

At times, retention opponents even co-opted slogans that liberal protesters have used this year to oppose the second Trump administration: one batch of Republican campaign signs read “[No Kings, No Retention](https://buckscountybeacon.com/2025/10/misleading-yard-signs-about-pennsylvania-supreme-court-election-pop-up-in-bucks-county/).”

The justices on the ballot this week campaigned aggressively in their own defense, touring the state and emphasizing that voting rights would be under threat should they lose.

“My court is the backstop of democracy,” Dougherty said at a September campaign event in Philadelphia.

Wecht defended his court’s decision to strike down the GOP-drawn congressional map in 2018. “It was a flamboyantly and really outrageously gerrymandered map,” he told _Bolts_.

_Bolts_[interviewed many Pennsylvania voters](https://boltsmag.org/pennsylvania-supreme-court-elections-2025/) in late September and found that all the campaigning and spending was failing to generate much anti-retention energy on the ground. One local party committee person from Lancaster County said state party leadership had failed to help leaders like herself make a clear, organized pitch to voters.

By Election Day, though, many millions of dollars more had poured into the state, and the heightened profile of this race may have broken through with more voters—just not in the way retention opponents had hoped. Plenty of red counties in Pennsylvania did vote against retention, but the justices ran up the numbers in bluer, more urban parts of the state.

Two lower-court judges, both Democrats, were up for retention as well on Tuesday in statewide races, and they were receiving similar results in preliminary returns as the three supreme court justices, though their races generated much less spending and attention.

Democrats also won two other statewide contests for Pennsylvania’s Commonwealth Court and Superior Court, two intermediate bodies. Those races were regular, partisan affairs, not retention elections.

“I appreciate the confidence that voters appear to be showing in me and my colleagues,” Wecht told _Bolts_.

Now, having failed to oust any of these justices, Republicans have a narrow path back to a court majority any time this decade. Three more seats on the court will go up for election in 2027. One Democrat (Debra Todd) and one Republican (Sallie Mundy) will each stand for retention that year. Plus, Donohue will need to leave the court because she’ll hit the age limit of 75, and her seat will be up for a regular, open race.

In the best-case scenario for Republicans, voters would retain Mundy, oust Todd, and elect a Republican to fill Donohue’s seat—but even that outcome would leave the court with a 3-3 tie.

![Image 2: Woman with blonde hair in a bun, wearing a blue jacket and silver necklace, waves her hands](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/25303575086534-scaled.jpg)

Christine Donohue won her retention race. She will be forced to retire by 2027. (AP Photo/Marc Levy)

In Pennsylvania, vacancies are filled by the governor, but two-thirds of the state Senate must vote to confirm a nominee. Even if the GOP flipped the governorship in 2026, it is very unlikely to also get a supermajority in the upper chamber. That could easily produce a stalemate. The last time a vacancy arose on this court, when Chief Justice Max Baer [died](https://boltsmag.org/pennsylvania-supreme-court-appointment-chief-justice/) in September 2022, the seat just remained empty until voters chose a replacement the following fall.

In the lead-up to Tuesday’s election, the justices facing retention argued that, should they not be retained, there’d be prolonged vacancies that’d create strong turbulence on the court. That scenario has been averted.

Aliza Shatzman, a Pennsylvania attorney who founded the Legal Accountability Project, a national organization and watchdog against court corruption, said the Democratic majority on the court can be “a bulwark against autocracy and federal overreach.”

She added, “I can’t think of a more important time to have a fully functioning seven-person Supreme Court than now, heading into the 2026 midterms.”

Three [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court "Pennsylvania Supreme Court") justices — [Christine Donohue](https://ballotpedia.org/Christine_Donohue "Christine Donohue") (D), [Kevin M. Dougherty](https://ballotpedia.org/Kevin_M._Dougherty "Kevin M. Dougherty") (D), and [David N. Wecht](https://ballotpedia.org/David_N._Wecht "David N. Wecht") (D) — were [retained](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention "Retention") in three elections held on November 4, 2025.

_WHYY_'s Carmen Russell-Sluchansky wrote, "State judicial elections typically garner little attention, but Pennsylvania’s 2025 state Supreme Court races are shaping up to be the next major political battleground."[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-1)

The state court had a 5-2 Democratic majority.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-2) At the time of the election, the court had been controlled by Democrats since [2015](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2015 "Pennsylvania Supreme Court elections, 2015"), when Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht won election to their seats.[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-3)

Pennsylvania used [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") to select a justice for an initial 10-year term, and used a [retention election](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to determine whether to keep them. If a justice was retained, they would serve another 10-year term. At the time of the election, Pennsylvania was one of eight states to use [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") for the initial selection of a justice and one of 22 to use [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") for the renewal of a term.

According to Pennsylvania's Code of Judicial Conduct, justices were limited in their ability to campaign.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-4) Both the Democratic and Republican parties said they would be involved in this race. The [Republican State Leadership Committee](https://ballotpedia.org/Republican_State_Leadership_Committee "Republican State Leadership Committee") ran ads on social media asking voters to vote against retaining the justices, which said, "In 2024, we voted by mail and flipped Pennsylvania red. This year, radical liberal judges are trying to secure another decade of power. We need you to stop them, show up again, vote 'no' in November."[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-5) The [Democratic National Committee](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") announced on September 25 that they would invest six figures in the final weeks of the race, and Democratic politicians including Gov. [Josh Shapiro](https://ballotpedia.org/Josh_Shapiro "Josh Shapiro") (D), Sen. [Elissa Slotkin](https://ballotpedia.org/Elissa_Slotkin "Elissa Slotkin") (D-Mich.), and Rep. [Chris Deluzio](https://ballotpedia.org/Chris_Deluzio "Chris Deluzio") (D) campaigned in favor of retention.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-7)

Since retention elections were established in 1968, only one Pennsylvania justice, Russell Nigro (D) in 2005, was not retained.[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-8) Since 2020, in 102 elections, 100 justices (**98%**) won retention. The most recent justice in the U.S. to not win retention was [Yvonne Kauger](https://ballotpedia.org/Yvonne_Kauger "Yvonne Kauger") in Oklahoma in [2024](https://ballotpedia.org/Oklahoma_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024 "Oklahoma Supreme Court elections, 2024").

_See also: [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania\_Supreme\_Court "Pennsylvania Supreme Court")_

Selection
---------

The **seven justices** of the [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court "Pennsylvania Supreme Court") are selected in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections").[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)

Justices serve 10-year terms, after which they must run in yes-no [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_elections "Retention elections") if they wish to remain on the court. A separate part of the ballot is designated for these elections, and justices' names appear without respect to party affiliation.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-retention-17) To learn more about these elections, visit the [Pennsylvania judicial elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_judicial_elections "Pennsylvania judicial elections") page.

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must:

*   have state residence for at least one year;
*   be a member of the state bar; and
*   be under the age of 75.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-new75-18)

### Chief justice

The [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court "Pennsylvania Supreme Court") chooses its chief justice by seniority; the title is held by the longest-serving justice on the court.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-code-19)

### Vacancies

_See also: [How vacancies are filled in state supreme courts](https://ballotpedia.org/How\_vacancies\_are\_filled\_in\_state\_supreme\_courts "How vacancies are filled in state supreme courts")_
In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [governor appoints a successor](https://ballotpedia.org/Gubernatorial_appointment_of_judges "Gubernatorial appointment of judges") who must be approved by a two-thirds vote of the [Pennsylvania Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Senate "Pennsylvania Senate"). Interim justices stand for election at the next municipal election occurring more than 10 months after the vacancy occurred.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)

By tradition, appointed interim judges of the supreme court, superior court, or court of appeals do not go on to run for permanent seats. In other words, the governor appoints these judges with the expectation that the judge will only fill the interim vacancy.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)
